query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a pack‐aluminization surface treatment to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloys will form a protective Al2O3 (alumina) scale that significantly improves the alloy’s oxygen resistance at high temperature without degrading its established mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Perform a pack‐aluminization treatment (a thermochemical process using an Al-rich pack) to deposit a thin aluminum-enriched surface layer that transforms into a continuous, adherent alumina scale.
generation.conditions: Expose the treated alloy to a high-temperature oxidizing environment (approximately 1000 °C) in air for an extended time (e.g., 100 hours) while subjecting it to strain rates on the order of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ during mechanical tests.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale formed on the alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: The formed aluminum oxide scale acts as a physical barrier reducing oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy during high-temperature exposure. This minimizes deleterious oxidation of the alloying elements, thereby preserving the alloy's mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated specimens will show a markedly lower weight gain (indicative of slower oxidation kinetics) than untreated samples when exposed to 1000 °C in air, while maintaining similar room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which oxidizes rapidly under high-temperature exposure in air, leading to performance degradation despite its initial ductility and strength properties.
generation.boundary: The outcome is expected primarily under high-temperature (around 1000 °C) static oxidation conditions in air with mechanical loading conditions similar to those already established (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹). The treatment must not introduce a brittle or excessively thick scale that could spall under mechanical stress.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal treatment parameters (temperature and duration of pack-aluminization, pack composition) and long-term scale stability under cyclic thermal/mechanical loading remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one group undergoes the pack‐aluminization treatment and the other remains untreated. Expose both groups to air at 1000 °C for 100 hours. After exposure, subject samples to room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength measurements.
measurements: Mass change (weight gain) during the oxidation test
Surface and cross-sectional analyses (using SEM/EDS) to verify the formation and integrity of the alumina scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminized samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in the oxidation rate (i.e., similar weight gain to untreated samples) or if they show a reduction in mechanical performance (e.g., decreased ductility or yield strength), the hypothesis will be falsified.
